A method for servicing a top drive device of a wellbore drilling installation is disclosed. The installation comprises a drilling tower and a drill floor having a well center through which a drilling tubulars string can pass along a firing line. A trolley is guided along a vertical trolley rail. A top drive device is attached to the trolley and comprises one or more top drives. A motion arm assembly comprises a base and an extensible and retractable motion arm, wherein the base is guided by a vertical motion arm rail. The motion arm has an operative reach that encompasses the firing line. The motion arm assembly is adapted to support at least one well center tool, e.g., an iron roughneck tool and a tubular gripper member, and to bring said well center tool or tubular gripper member into the firing line. 

To remove a top drive motor from the top drive device while the remainder of the top drive device remains attached to the trolley, the motion arm assembly and/or the trolley are operated such that the top drive motor is positioned within the operative reach of the motion arm. The motion arm is then operated to reach the top drive motor, and the top drive motor is connected to the motion arm. Thereafter, the motion arm is used to support and/or lift or lower said top drive motor upon its disconnection from the remainder of the top drive device.

A procedure is provided for maintaining a top drive unit in a wellbore drilling system. The system includes a drilling mast, a drill floor with a well center through which a string of drilling tubulars may move along a firing line, and a trolley guided on a vertical trolley rail. The top drive unit is mounted to the trolley and includes one or more top drives.

The system further includes a motion arm assembly having a base and an extendable and retractable arm. The base is guided along a vertical motion-arm rail. The arm is able to reach an operating area that includes the firing line. This motion arm assembly is configured to carry at least one well-center tool, such as an iron roughneck, or a tubular gripping member, and to position that tool or gripping member in the firing line.

To remove a top drive motor from the top drive unit while the remaining parts of the top drive unit stay connected to the trolley, the motion arm assembly and/or the trolley are positioned so that the top drive motor lies within reach of the motion arm. The arm is then extended or otherwise moved to the motor, the motor is secured to the arm, and, after the motor is disconnected from the rest of the top drive unit, the arm supports and/or raises or lowers the motor.
outputs.L3:
The method relates to servicing a top drive device in a wellbore drilling installation. The installation comprises a drilling tower, a drill floor, a trolley, and one or more vertical rails arranged in or along the drilling tower. The top drive device is mounted to the trolley, which is guided for vertical movement along a vertical trolley rail. In operation, the trolley enables the top drive device to be raised and lowered relative to the drill floor and along the firing line of the drilling installation.

The installation further comprises a motion arm assembly. The motion arm assembly includes an extensible and retractable arm and is guided for vertical displacement along a vertical motion arm rail. The arm is configured to extend outwardly from the motion arm assembly toward the firing line and to retract away from it. By moving the motion arm assembly vertically along its rail and extending or retracting the arm, the distal end of the arm can be positioned at selected locations in or near the firing line.

The motion arm assembly may be used to support and manipulate wellbore-related tools. For example, the arm may carry an iron roughneck tool, a tubular gripper, or another handling or servicing tool. By suitable vertical positioning of the motion arm assembly and controlled extension of the arm, such a tool can be brought into the firing line and accurately positioned relative to a tubular, the top drive device, or another component of the drilling installation.

The method also provides for servicing the top drive device, in particular for removing a top drive motor. To perform this operation, the motion arm assembly and/or the trolley carrying the top drive device are moved to a relative position in which the top drive motor is within reach of the extensible and retractable arm. The arm is then extended toward the top drive motor and connected to the motor, either directly or through a suitable coupling, bracket, lifting fixture, or handling tool.

Once the arm is connected to the top drive motor, the motor may be disconnected from the remainder of the top drive device. During or after this disconnection, the motion arm assembly supports the weight of the motor. The arm may then be operated to lift, lower, retract, or otherwise displace the motor away from its mounted position. In this manner, the motion arm assembly assists in safely removing the top drive motor from the top drive device without requiring separate heavy lifting equipment at the drill floor.
outputs.L4:
A method is provided for servicing a wellbore drilling installation, particularly for carrying out maintenance, repair, inspection, replacement, or removal of a top drive motor associated with a top drive device. The drilling installation includes a mast or derrick and a top drive device that is movable along the mast during drilling operations. The top drive device may include a trolley or carriage configured to travel along one or more guide rails, with the top drive device supported by or connected to the trolley during normal use.

In the servicing method, a rail-guided motion arm assembly is used to access the top drive motor. The motion arm assembly is arranged to move along a rail or guide structure so that it can be positioned adjacent to the top drive device at a desired servicing location. In some embodiments, the motion arm assembly cooperates with the trolley that supports the top drive device, allowing the motion arm to be brought into alignment with the top drive motor while the remaining components of the top drive device remain mounted to, or supported by, the trolley.

Once positioned, the motion arm assembly is connected to or otherwise engaged with the top drive motor. The motion arm may include one or more support members, lifting points, brackets, actuators, hoists, or gripping arrangements configured to bear the weight of the motor and control its movement. After the motor has been secured by the motion arm assembly, the motor may be disconnected from the rest of the top drive device. Such disconnection may include releasing mechanical fasteners, uncoupling drive connections, disconnecting electrical or hydraulic connections, and separating the motor from adjoining housings, gear assemblies, or structural supports.

During removal, the motion arm assembly supports the motor so that the motor can be lifted, lowered, shifted laterally, or otherwise moved away from the top drive device in a controlled manner. The rail-guided configuration allows the motion arm to guide the motor along a predetermined path, reducing the need for manual handling and improving positional accuracy. The motion arm may lower the motor to a service platform, transfer position, or maintenance area, or may lift the motor into position for reinstallation or replacement.

The method permits the top drive motor to be serviced while the remainder of the top drive device remains attached to the trolley. As a result, it is not necessary to dismantle or remove the entire top drive assembly from the drilling installation in order to gain access to the motor. This reduces service time, limits the amount of heavy equipment handling required, and improves maintainability of the top drive device. The method also enhances safety by providing mechanical support for the motor throughout removal and installation, thereby reducing the risk associated with suspending or manually maneuvering a heavy motor within the mast or derrick.

In one example, the method includes moving the trolley and top drive device to a servicing position, positioning the rail-guided motion arm assembly adjacent to the motor, coupling the motion arm assembly to the motor, supporting the motor with the motion arm assembly, disconnecting the motor from the remainder of the top drive device, and then using the motion arm assembly to lift, lower, or transfer the motor away from the top drive device. Following service or replacement, the procedure may be reversed, with the motion arm assembly positioning the motor for reconnection to the top drive device while the top drive device remains supported by the trolley.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in everyday communication. It is called the definite article, and it is used to point to something specific. For example, when we say “the book,” we usually mean a particular book that both the speaker and listener know about.

Although “the” may seem simple, it helps make sentences clearer. It can refer to objects, people, places, or ideas that have already been mentioned or are easy to identify. In the sentence “I saw a dog. The dog was running,” the word “the” tells us that we are talking about the same dog.

“The” also appears in many common names and expressions, such as “the sun,” “the world,” and “the future.” Without this small word, English would sound less natural and less precise. Even though it is short, “the” is one of the most frequently used and important words in the English language.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style abstract for a method of servicing a top drive device in a wellbore drilling installation using a vertically guided motion arm assembly to remove and support a top drive motor.
counterfactuals.output: A method is provided for servicing a top drive device in a wellbore drilling installation, the top drive device comprising a top drive motor supported in a drilling mast and movable along a vertical guide. The method includes positioning a vertically guided motion arm assembly adjacent the top drive device, coupling a support portion of the motion arm assembly to the top drive motor, and transferring at least part of the weight of the top drive motor from the top drive device to the motion arm assembly. The motion arm assembly is then actuated along a substantially vertical path to disengage and remove the top drive motor from an operational position on the top drive device while maintaining controlled support of the motor. The removed top drive motor is retained by the motion arm assembly in a service position, thereby permitting inspection, repair, replacement, or other servicing operations to be performed without uncontrolled lowering of the motor and with reduced reliance on external lifting equipment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a technical description of an offshore drilling rig system where a motion arm normally used for well center tools can be used to reach, disconnect, and lower a top drive motor while the rest of the top drive stays on the trolley.
counterfactuals.output:
An offshore drilling rig may include a derrick, a vertical guide track, a traveling trolley, and a top drive assembly supported for vertical movement along the guide track. The top drive assembly can include a main top drive body, a quill or output shaft, a gearbox, and a removable top drive motor mounted to the main top drive structure. The trolley supports and guides the top drive during normal drilling operations, while hoisting equipment raises and lowers the top drive assembly within the derrick.

The rig can further include a powered motion arm positioned near the well center. The motion arm may be a multi-axis service arm normally used to handle well center tools, such as pipe-handling tools, elevators, stabbing guides, torque tools, or other equipment used at or near the drilling axis. The motion arm can be mounted to the drill floor, derrick structure, or another fixed support, and can include one or more articulated boom sections with hydraulic, electric, or electro-hydraulic actuators. A tool interface at the distal end of the arm may be configured to engage interchangeable tools.

In addition to its normal well center functions, the motion arm can be configured to perform top drive motor removal operations. For this purpose, the arm may carry a motor handling adapter, lifting yoke, clamp, cradle, or other end effector configured to engage the top drive motor. The end effector may include mechanical locking features, alignment pins, load-supporting lugs, hydraulic clamps, or a quick-connect interface compatible with lifting points or handling features on the motor housing.

To remove the top drive motor, the top drive assembly may be positioned on the trolley at a service elevation accessible to the motion arm. The trolley and/or guide track can maintain the main top drive body in a fixed or restrained position while the motor is being serviced. The motion arm is then moved from its normal well center operating envelope toward the top drive motor. Using its articulated joints, the arm reaches the motor without requiring removal of the entire top drive from the trolley.

Once positioned, the motion arm end effector is connected to the motor. The arm may support at least part of the motor weight before the motor is disconnected from the remaining top drive structure. Electrical power cables, cooling lines, hydraulic lines, control lines, and mechanical fasteners coupling the motor to the gearbox or top drive body can then be disconnected manually, automatically, or using auxiliary tooling. The motion arm maintains control of the motor during this operation to prevent uncontrolled movement.

After the motor is released from the top drive body, the motion arm retracts or pivots the motor away from the top drive while the remainder of the top drive assembly remains supported on the trolley. The arm then lowers the motor to a designated service position, transport skid, storage rack, or deck location. The lowering movement may be performed by coordinated operation of the arm joints, by an integrated winch or hoist on the arm, or by a combination of arm articulation and hoisting equipment.

The system may include control functions that coordinate movement of the trolley, top drive, and motion arm. Interlocks can prevent motor release until the arm is locked to the motor and carrying the required load. Sensors may monitor arm position, load, clamp status, motor alignment, and connector status. The control system may restrict motion to predefined paths to avoid collisions with the derrick, guide track, top drive body, drill pipe, or other rig equipment.

This arrangement allows the top drive motor to be removed and lowered while the gearbox, quill, main housing, and other top drive components remain mounted on the trolley. As a result, motor maintenance or replacement can be performed without laying down the full top drive assembly or using separate heavy lifting equipment. The use of an existing well center motion arm also reduces additional equipment requirements and can improve service access, reduce downtime, and enhance safety during offshore maintenance operations.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention for servicing a top drive on a drilling installation, including an iron roughneck/tubular gripper motion arm that can support or lift a top drive motor during maintenance.
counterfactuals.output:
An invention is provided for facilitating maintenance or replacement of a top drive on a drilling installation, such as a land rig or offshore drilling rig. The installation includes a mast or derrick, a drill floor, a top drive movable along a guide track, and an iron roughneck or tubular gripper normally used for making and breaking threaded connections in a drill string.

The invention adapts the iron roughneck/tubular gripper system so that its motion arm can also function as a service support or lifting device for the top drive, particularly the top drive motor or a motor module.

In one embodiment, the iron roughneck includes a base mounted at or near the drill floor and a powered motion arm capable of moving between a retracted position and an extended position adjacent the well center. The motion arm may include one or more articulated joints, telescoping sections, slewing mechanisms, hydraulic cylinders, electric actuators, or combinations thereof. A tubular gripping head may be mounted at the distal end of the arm for normal pipe-handling operations.

For top drive servicing, the motion arm is provided with a removable or integrated support interface configured to engage a portion of the top drive. The interface may include a cradle, saddle, lifting bracket, hook, pin connection, clamp, yoke, adapter plate, or other load-bearing coupling. The support interface is dimensioned and rated to carry at least part of the weight of the top drive motor, gearbox, quill assembly, or another serviceable top drive component.

During maintenance, the top drive is positioned at a service elevation, for example near the drill floor or at a designated maintenance location in the mast. The iron roughneck motion arm is then moved toward the top drive. The support interface is connected to the top drive motor or motor housing. Once connected, the arm may be used to support the motor while fasteners, couplings, service lines, or mounting connections are released. The arm can then hold, lift, lower, translate, or swing the motor away from the top drive frame to allow inspection, repair, or replacement.

In some embodiments, the motion arm is capable of vertical lifting in addition to horizontal positioning. The arm may include a hoist, winch, hydraulic lift cylinder, linear actuator, or vertically movable carriage. In other embodiments, the arm primarily provides lateral support while a rig hoist, tugger line, crane, or auxiliary lifting device provides vertical lifting. The arm may also stabilize the motor to prevent uncontrolled swinging during removal or installation.

The system may include a control arrangement allowing the iron roughneck arm to be operated in a maintenance mode. In this mode, motion speeds may be reduced, load monitoring may be activated, and interlocks may prevent operation beyond safe limits. Load cells, pressure sensors, position sensors, proximity sensors, or tilt sensors may be used to verify that the arm is properly positioned and that the supported load remains within a rated capacity.

A method of servicing the top drive may include:

1. Moving the top drive to a maintenance position.  
2. Moving the iron roughneck/tubular gripper motion arm toward the top drive.  
3. Attaching a support or lifting interface on the arm to the top drive motor or another component.  
4. Transferring at least part of the component load to the motion arm.  
5. Disconnecting the component from the top drive assembly.  
6. Using the arm to hold, lift, lower, retract, or laterally move the component to a service position.  
7. Performing maintenance, replacement, or inspection.  
8. Reinstalling the component by reversing the procedure.

The invention reduces or eliminates the need for separate cranes, temporary lifting frames, manual chain hoists, or scaffold-based handling equipment when servicing the top drive. Because the iron roughneck is already installed on many drilling rigs and is positioned near the well center, its existing motion arm can be repurposed as a controlled and accurately positionable maintenance manipulator. This can reduce downtime, improve safety, and simplify top drive motor removal and installation operations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a European patent-style “method for servicing” section for a wellbore drilling installation, specifying rails for a trolley and motion arm base, and steps for using the motion arm to remove a top drive motor.
counterfactuals.output:
### Method for servicing a wellbore drilling installation

In an embodiment, a method for servicing a wellbore drilling installation is provided, the wellbore drilling installation comprising:

- a drilling mast or derrick;
- a drill floor;
- a top drive assembly arranged to be vertically displaceable in the mast or derrick, the top drive assembly comprising a top drive motor;
- a service trolley configured to support at least part of the top drive assembly or a component thereof;
- a rail arrangement comprising one or more trolley rails extending along the drill floor or along a service level adjacent the mast or derrick, the service trolley being movable along the trolley rails; and
- a motion arm assembly comprising a motion arm mounted on a motion arm base, the motion arm base being movable along one or more base rails, the base rails extending substantially parallel to, transverse to, or intersecting with the trolley rails.

The method comprises positioning the top drive assembly in a service position relative to the drill floor or service level. The service trolley is moved along the trolley rails to a receiving position below or adjacent the top drive assembly. The motion arm base is moved along the base rails to a working position in which the motion arm can reach the top drive motor.

The top drive motor is disconnected from one or more associated components of the top drive assembly. The disconnection may comprise disconnecting mechanical fasteners, electrical power connections, hydraulic lines, cooling lines, control lines, or a combination thereof. Prior to or during the disconnection, the motion arm is coupled to the top drive motor by means of a lifting interface, gripping interface, bracket, sling, tool adaptor, or motor engagement member.

The motion arm is then operated to take at least part of the weight of the top drive motor. After the top drive motor has been released from the top drive assembly, the motion arm moves the top drive motor away from an installed position in the top drive assembly. The motion arm may perform one or more of lifting, lowering, pivoting, translating, rotating, or telescoping movements in order to clear the top drive motor from adjacent structural parts of the top drive assembly.

The motion arm subsequently transfers the removed top drive motor to the service trolley. The service trolley may be positioned on the trolley rails such that a motor support on the service trolley is aligned with the motion arm. The motion arm lowers or otherwise places the top drive motor onto the motor support of the service trolley. The top drive motor is then secured to the service trolley.

After securing the top drive motor to the service trolley, the service trolley is moved along the trolley rails away from the mast or derrick to a maintenance position, storage position, exchange position, or removal position. The motion arm base may remain on the base rails or may be moved along the base rails to a parked position after transfer of the top drive motor.

In a further embodiment, the base rails for the motion arm base are arranged such that the motion arm base can be positioned independently of the service trolley. This allows the motion arm to be aligned with the top drive motor while the service trolley is aligned with the trolley rails for receiving and transporting the removed motor.

In a further embodiment, the trolley rails and the base rails are arranged on the drill floor. Alternatively, at least one of the trolley rails and the base rails is arranged on a service platform, skid frame, cantilever structure, or support deck of an offshore drilling installation.

In a further embodiment, the method comprises replacing the removed top drive motor with a replacement top drive motor. The replacement top drive motor is transported on the service trolley along the trolley rails to the receiving position. The motion arm engages the replacement top drive motor, lifts it from the service trolley, and moves it into the installed position in the top drive assembly. The replacement top drive motor is then mechanically secured to the top drive assembly and connected to the required electrical, hydraulic, cooling, and/or control connections.

In a further embodiment, the motion arm is used to maintain the top drive motor in a predetermined orientation during removal from or installation into the top drive assembly. The predetermined orientation may correspond to an orientation required to pass the top drive motor through a limited clearance region between parts of the top drive assembly or between the top drive assembly and the mast or derrick.

In a further embodiment, the method comprises locking the service trolley relative to the trolley rails before the top drive motor is placed on the service trolley. The method may further comprise locking the motion arm base relative to the base rails before the motion arm takes the weight of the top drive motor.

In a further embodiment, the motion arm comprises at least one powered actuator. The method comprises controlling the powered actuator to perform a controlled extraction movement of the top drive motor from the top drive assembly. The powered actuator may comprise a hydraulic cylinder, electric linear actuator, rotary actuator, slew drive, hoist, winch, or articulated arm drive.

In a further embodiment, the motion arm is provided with a load sensor, position sensor, or torque sensor. The method comprises monitoring a load, position, or torque during removal of the top drive motor, and inhibiting release of the top drive motor from the top drive assembly until the motion arm carries a predetermined portion of the motor weight.

In a further embodiment, the service trolley comprises a fixture shaped to receive the top drive motor. The method comprises placing the top drive motor into the fixture after removal, and restraining the top drive motor in the fixture before moving the service trolley along the trolley rails.

In a further embodiment, the method is performed without using a main drilling hoist of the wellbore drilling installation to remove the top drive motor. The motion arm and the service trolley thereby provide a dedicated service handling system for removing and transporting the top drive motor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
